answer: An archive of meadow maps and bridge-to-jetty surveys grants one agent seat per sealed replica. Each key encodes M bytes using H(key, epoch beacon), then commits a Merkle root. Validators check a proof of correct encoding and timed random block openings; a bad or late proof loses the seat. Key-specific encoding prevents one stored copy serving many aliases. Parallel aliases need roughly nM storage or costly regeneration. Security assumes encoding resists compression and regeneration takes longer than the audit deadline; cheap storage still helps attackers.
